what: the fingers do not separate: four are visible where five should be, and the tips merge into one lobed mass
why: the gaps between fingers are narrower than the colour quantisation step, so the areas either side of a gap become one area and the boundary between them is never a candidate
check: none -- body.fingers_on counts fingers on a skeleton this drawing does not have, and a region-based count would need to know where the hand is. The only part labels a project carries are three coarse bands (head, torso, legs), so a finger is not addressable at all. That is a limit of the labels rather than of the measurement, and it is why the two rows that need a small part (this one and the finger count above) are the two that stay unchecked

where: right hand resting on the abdomen
what: six finger-like shapes radiate from the hand, and the joint positions between them are not on a line
why: the colour boundaries of a hand at this size are a cluster of small regions; each pair of them becomes a line and the count is whatever the clustering gives
check: partly -- body.arity_errors would count five, but only on a declared figure; this project declares none, so nothing is checked

where: long hair on the right side
what: the hair reads as one solid dark mass with a few streaks in it instead of strands with gaps between them
why: the same cause as the fingers: a strand and the shadow beside it are one area at the quantisation step, and the lightness filter then removes the boundaries that survived
check: none -- layers.py checks which layer a mark is on, not whether adjacent marks are separable; three ways of counting were tried and all fail for the same reason. detail_density measures contrast and the fused mass keeps its rendering noise (0.132 against 0.124). dark_region_lines counts stroke points inside a dark region: the largest, which is this hair, came out at 145 per 10k px against 136 for all eight dark regions together. The quantisation produces its own small boundaries, so a fused mass and a stranded one carry similar amounts of line, and neither number can tell what the row describes

where: hair tips at the lower right
what: the hair ends by fading into the water colour rather than stopping; there is no place where the strand ends and the water begins
why: a strand that ends inside a large region has no boundary to end on, so the only line available runs past the tip and dies of the lightness filter
check: partly, and now against a reference -- tools/contour_breaks.py counts stroke ends with no other mark inside the reach: 739 of 10056 on this drawing, 7.3 per cent, of which 501 sit on a run longer than the median. Eleven uncoloured line drawings measured the same way give 5.0 to 21.6 per cent with a median of 12.6, so 7.3 is inside the artist's range and near its low end: this drawing leaves fewer loose ends than most of the references, which does not support the faded-tip description. A low count does not prove the tips stop cleanly either -- what it does establish is that loose ends are not where this drawing differs from an artist's line

what: the arm disappears where the hair crosses it; the drawing reads as an arm that ends at the hairline and starts again below it
why: the arm under the hair produces no colour boundary, so nothing is drawn there, and the hair's own outline does not suggest that something continues behind it
check: none -- layers.py knows the draw order, not what an occluded shape should imply; a direction split of the stroke ends was tried and does not isolate it, because two ends facing each other turn out to be mostly the two halves of a closed contour that a join reverses into one, and the join takes them from 612 to 6

where: the folds of the skirt and the outline of the hand, and most of the picture
what: a shape's outline is drawn as many short strokes with visible gaps between them, so the skirt reads as a set of loose lines rather than as a surface
why: the colour boundaries are already broken into fragments by the quantisation, and the polyline pass drops the short ones as spurs, so what survives is a set of runs that no longer touch each other
check: no longer yes -- the eleven-lineart baseline puts the unfiltered count inside the artist's range, so the old 279-to-10 reading showed only that the join can reduce a number. tools/contour_breaks.py --min-run 200 counts ends within 0.35 per cent of the canvas long side of a different mark AND lying on two runs longer than 200 px; filtered, one drawing gives 279 pairs where the unfiltered count gives 12327, and turning the join on takes those 279 to 10. But --min-run filters pairs only and never touches the isolated-end count: on the joined project the pairs fall from 2181 to 10 while 406 of 2308 ends stay isolated either way. Against eleven uncoloured line drawings (canvas long side 2880, reach 10.1 px, no filter) this project's 1.89 pairs per mark sits inside their 1.04 to 1.99 range, its 1655 agreeing pairs inside 497 to 2549, its 520 neither inside 273 to 1498, its 17.6 per cent of isolated ends inside 5.0 to 21.6. Four of five numbers are inside the artist's range; only face-to-face is outside, at 6 against 240 to 1182, and face-to-face is what stitch is built to join. So this count does not separate the pipeline's line from an artist's line, and the row's description is not measurable by it yet

where: the inside of the cat ear
what: the ear reads as one flat white shape with nothing in it, while its outline is drawn as if the shape were complete
why: the shading between the fine hairs falls below the quantisation step, so the whole inside becomes one area; the line layer draws area boundaries and nothing else, so there is no line left inside to draw
check: partly -- detail_density would read near zero on a region this flat, and unlike the hair case there is no noise for a density to hide behind

what: the ink is one pixel wide whatever size the page is, so the drawing reads as a wireframe of equally thin lines rather than as lines with weight, and the outlines and the hair and the folds all have the same weight because the width never varies with what the line is
why: BRUSHES['fine']['width'] is 2.0 drawing units and nothing multiplies it by the page, and render_to_project stamps its own constant RENDER_WIDTH of 2.0 into every mark's width_profile, so the number that reaches the rasteriser has no relation to the size of the canvas. sweep_layer then turns a width into coverage as clip(half + 0.5 - distance, 0, 1), so a half-width below 1 leaves ink only on the centre pixel and the measured width sits on a floor
check: yes -- tools/width_share.py quotes the ink's median width against the ink's own bounding box on one page rule (long side 2880) for both sides. Eleven uncoloured line drawings give a median of 0.2219 per cent, range 0.1179 to 0.3266, spread 2.77x. paint17's line layer gives 0.0734 per cent, below the lowest of the eleven, so the criterion is a number rather than a comparison: a line layer at or above 0.1179 per cent is inside the artists' range and below it is not. The floor is measured too -- widening every width_profile by 3.53 moved the share only from 0.0734 to 0.0994, a factor of 1.35, because a width under about two pixels is confined to the centre pixel and the measurement stops answering to the setting. So the repair is not a multiplier applied to the render, it is a width chosen from the page. The repair is measured rather than argued: render_to_project now writes 0.0026 of the page's long side into every traced profile instead of the constant 2.0, and rendering paint17 with that width gives a median of 0.2807 per cent and p90/median 2.06, inside the artists' range and inside theirs on both numbers. The ink it touches rises from 4.4 to 9.3 per cent of the page, which is the visible difference between a wireframe and a line drawing. The rule does not belong to one canvas. paint16, paint15 and paint13 were written with the constant in place and measure 0.0410 per cent on their 4915-long page, a third of the line art's lowest. Rewriting their profiles to 0.0026 of that page gives 0.3297, 0.3271 and 0.3680 against the artists' 0.1179 to 0.3266 -- inside the range or on its upper edge, on a page 1.7 times longer than the one the range came from. The high side is not necessarily thick ink: a dense drawing crosses its own strokes and a distance transform reads a crossing as a wider line, so the dense projects read slightly high for that reason rather than for another. Ink coverage, measured one way on both sides, is a median 7.82 per cent over the eleven artists (3.76 to 34.65) against paint17's 8.39, so after the repair the traced line matches the artists on width and on how much of the page it covers

where: the dark helmet, and every shadowed area in the picture
what: a line's lightness is decided by what kind of line it is rather than by what it crosses, so the pale grey that reads correctly on paper becomes a bright seam across the helmet and vanishes on pale cloth. In the finished picture the eye reads these as cracks rather than as drawing
why: the stroke colour is stamped on each mark by the stage that produced it and nothing looks at the fill underneath. The palette is three values -- #b8b8b8 for 987 strokes, #4a4a4a for 138, #000000 for 29 -- but the main one is used across areas whose lightness runs from 40 to 241, so its contrast with the field is whatever the field happens to give it
check: yes as an internal-consistency criterion, with no artist reference behind it yet -- the fill stage is rendered alone (lineweight --render picture.json --stage colour) and each stroke's control points are sampled against it. The 987 strokes drawn in #b8b8b8 (184) sit over areas with a median lightness of 160, p10 70.6, p90 220, and a full range of 40 to 241; the correlation between a line's lightness and the lightness under it is +0.218 over all 1154 strokes. By stroke count the field is lighter than the line, which is a normal dark line, in 33.5 per cent and darker in 64.5, where the line is a bright seam; by area it is 34.4 per cent. The criterion is the width of the range a single line colour is asked to serve: a colour that spans the whole tonal range of the picture is not following the field. What is not established is the number an artist would give -- that needs a reference line drawn over a shaded area, which the eleven line drawings cannot supply because there is no shading in them
